New York Times Co. v. Sullivan. The 1964 Supreme Court decision establishing that public officials suing for libel must prove actual malice, that a statement was made with knowledge of its falsity or with reckless disregard for the truth. L.B. Sullivan, a Montgomery, Alabama police commissioner, sued The New York Times for a 1960 advertisement criticizing his department's response to civil rights protests. Alabama's libel law allowed recovery for defamatory falsehoods, and the Times would have been liable even for minor factual errors.

Justice William Brennan held that the First Amendment requires public officials to prove actual malice, knowledge or reckless disregard of falsity, to recover damages. The decision applied to criticism of official conduct, recognizing that the public's right to criticize government outweighs reputation interests. It shielded newspapers and media from crippling libel suits, enabling fearless reporting on government and public figures. The doctrine extended in Curtis Publishing Co. v. Butts in 1967 to public figures more broadly, not just officials. The decision transformed legal standards for defamation and fundamentally protected the press's role as a check on power.
